chief_complaint: deep partial and full-thickness thermal burns covering 35% of body surface area after propane explosion
hpi_details: 36M industrial worker injured when a propane tank exploded in an enclosed workshop. Sustained direct flame burns to anterior trunk, bilateral entire upper extremities, and face. Experienced singed nasal hairs and carbonaceous sputum. Brought by helicopter EMS 1 hour post-injury.
ideas: in severe agony complaining of burning skin and difficulty breathing
concerns: worried about facial disfigurement, limb loss, and survival
expectations: wants immediate pain relief, burn wound care, and sedation

investigation_events.title: STAT co-oximetry and lactate
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT co-oximetry and lactate results are now available. Continue high-flow oxygen and do not delay early airway control or burn resuscitation.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Thermal Burn Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Thermal Burn Injury is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes airway protection, Parkland formula fluid resuscitation, and escharotomy for circumferential burns with transfer to a burn unit, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: deep partial and full-thickness thermal burns covering 35% of body surface area after propane explosion

Key HPI features: 36M industrial worker injured when a propane tank exploded in an enclosed workshop. Sustained direct flame burns to anterior trunk, bilateral entire upper extremities, and face. Experienced singed nasal hairs and carbonaceous sputum. Brought by helicopter EMS 1 hour post-injury.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 128, BP 100/65, RR 26, SpO2 93% on non-rebreather mask. Facial burns with singed eyebrows/nasal hairs, carbonaceous soot in oropharynx, and hoarseness (inhalation injury). Wound assessment using Lund-Browder chart / Rule of Nines: Anterior torso (18%) and bilateral upper extremities (18%) show mixed deep partial-thickness (blistering, cherry red/mottled, sluggish capillary refill) and full-thickness (leathery, pearly white, insensate) burns. Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) burned is 36%. Circumferential full-thickness burn noted on right forearm with tight, inelastic eschar and decreasing radial pulse.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Thermal Burn Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chemical burn without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inhalation injury (soot in mouth, hoarseness).
management_principles: STAT emergency management: secure the airway, resuscitate with fluids, and relieve any circumferential constriction.
Early endotracheal intubation for airway protection given facial burns/hoarseness before severe edema supervenes

Initiate Parkland Formula fluid resuscitation using Lactated Ringer's solution: 4 mL x 70 kg x 36% TBSA = ~10,080 mL in first 24 hours (give half [5,040 mL] in first 8 hours post-injury, titrating to urine output > 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr via Foley catheter)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: deep partial and full-thickness thermal burns covering 35% of body surface area after propane explosion

36M industrial worker injured when a propane tank exploded in an enclosed workshop. Sustained direct flame burns to anterior trunk, bilateral entire upper extremities, and face. Experienced singed nasal hairs and carbonaceous sputum. Brought by helicopter EMS 1 hour post-injury.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 128, BP 100/65, RR 26, SpO2 93% on non-rebreather mask. Facial burns with singed eyebrows/nasal hairs, carbonaceous soot in oropharynx, and hoarseness (inhalation injury). Wound assessment using Lund-Browder chart / Rule of Nines: Anterior torso (18%) and bilateral upper extremities (18%) show mixed deep partial-thickness (blistering, cherry red/mottled, sluggish capillary refill) and full-thickness (leathery, pearly white, insensate) burns. Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) burned is 36%. Circumferential full-thickness burn noted on right forearm with tight, inelastic eschar and decreasing radial pulse.
reference_soap.assessment: Severe Thermal Burns covering 36% TBSA with Inhalation Injury and Right Forearm Circumferential Eschar compartment risk.
reference_soap.plan: STAT burn-center management: secure the airway early for progressive inhalation-injury risk; calculate resuscitation from the documented weight and burn size, then titrate lactated Ringer's to physiologic endpoints. Perform escharotomy only when serial neurovascular/perfusion assessment confirms constriction, by an appropriately trained burn/trauma clinician. Transfer urgently to a verified burn unit for definitive wound care.

learning_objectives: Calculate burn Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) accurately using the Wallace Rule of Nines and Lund-Browder charts
Apply the Parkland / Modified Brooke resuscitation formulas (Lactated Ringer's titration based on urine output targets)
Recognize critical clinical indications for early preventive airway intubation in inhalation injuries (singed facial hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor)
Differentiate escharotomy indications from fasciotomy in circumferential full-thickness extremity burns

teaching.one_liner: Tissue injury caused by heat exposure, requiring assessment of total body surface area (TBSA), depth, and airway involvement.

must_ask.say: What caused the burn — open flame, hot liquid, steam, or chemicals?
Were you trapped in an enclosed space, and do you have hoarseness or black soot in your cough?
Which body parts were burned — face, chest, arms, or legs?
Are the burned areas extremely painful and blistered, or numb and white?
Did you cool the burn with clean tap water and have you received IV fluids?

history.answer: Please help me, a propane tank exploded in my workshop! My chest and arms are burning alive, and I can barely breathe!
I was repairing a valve when a propane tank suddenly exploded and engulfed me in a massive fireball.
The explosion happened about one hour ago, and the flight crew flew me straight here in the helicopter.
The flames hit my face, my entire chest and belly, and both of my arms.
Yes, I was working inside an enclosed, poorly ventilated workshop when the tank blew up.
Yes, my throat feels swollen and tight, and it is getting harder and harder to pull in enough air.
My voice has become really raspy and hoarse over the past half hour.
Yes, I had coughing fits right after the blast and coughed up dark black soot.
It was propane gas fire; the direct flames blasted me for several seconds before I could escape.
My coworkers smothered the flames with a heavy blanket; they did not pour cold water or anything on it.
The helicopter paramedics put an oxygen mask over my face and started an IV line in my leg to pump fluids.
The burns on my chest and left arm hurt like hell, a ten out of ten, but parts of my right forearm feel weirdly numb.
My right forearm feels completely rigid and tight, and my right hand is tingling and hard to open or close.
No, I didn't get hit by flying metal and I'm not bleeding; the skin is just blistered and peeling.
No dirt, rusty debris, chemicals, or animal bites touched the burns, just the fire and black smoke.
No, there is no pus, foul smell, or spreading redness; the accident happened just an hour ago.
No, I have never had chronic ulcers, bedsores, or wounds that wouldn't heal.
I am on my feet working every single day; I am not bedridden or confined to a chair.
No, this was purely an unexpected workplace blast, not violence or anyone trying to hurt me.
I feel like my skin is still scorching and my windpipe is closing up on me.
I am terrified that I might lose my right arm, end up terribly disfigured, or stop breathing and die.
I need you to give me something strong for this pain, help me breathe, and save my arms.
I don't have any chronic illnesses; no diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries and have never spent a night in a hospital before today.
I do not take any prescription pills, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or materials like latex.
I think I had a tetanus booster shot about seven or eight years ago after a cut at work.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink a beer or two occasionally on weekends, nothing heavy.
I work as a chemical plant mechanic and live at home with my wife.
Both of my parents are alive and healthy; there is no major disease running in my family.

exam.finding: Diaphoretic, visibly anxious male in acute distress, propped upright, tachypneic with audible hoarseness.
Heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93% on non-rebreather mask, and temperature 36.8°C.
Singed nasal hairs and eyebrows, soot deposited across the posterior oropharynx, mucosal edema, and a raspy, hoarse voice.
Tachypneic respirations with mild upper-airway stridor and scattered coarse breath sounds bilaterally, without focal crackles.
Rapid regular rhythm without audible murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Deep partial-thickness blistering burns on the anterior torso and left upper extremity, with leathery, pearly-white full-thickness eschar covering approximately 36% total body surface area.
Tight circumferential eschar on the right forearm with a markedly diminished, sluggish right radial pulse compared to the full left radial pulse.
Marked loss of light touch and pinprick sensation over the right hand and digits, while sensation in the lower extremities is fully preserved.
Impaired active finger flexion and extension in the right hand due to severe tenseness of the forearm compartment, with normal motor strength in the lower extremities.
